title: The Fourth Voyage of Sindbad
summary: Sindbad related the strange events of his fourth voyage:
full_text:
Sindbad related the strange events of his fourth voyage:

'Shipwrecked once again on a tropical coast, my companions and I were captured by a tribe of savages who fed the captives a strange herb that robbed them of their reason, fattening them for the pot. Recognizing the danger, I refused to eat the herb, surviving on wild berries until my wits remained clear, and escaped through the forest.

After eight days of wandering, I reached the civilized kingdom of King Mihrjan. Observing that the king and his nobles rode their fine horses bareback without saddles or stirrups, I engaged a master carpenter and leather-worker, fashioning the first padded saddle with polished stirrups seen in that realm.

The king and court were delighted, and I was rewarded with vast estates and given a noble maiden in marriage.

We lived in supreme happiness until my beloved wife fell ill of a sudden fever and died. Only then did I learn the dreadful custom of that kingdom: when a husband or wife died, the surviving spouse was buried alive beside the deceased in a colossal subterranean cave beneath the mountain!

The citizens escorted me with funeral solemnity, lowered me into the dark cavern with a pitcher of water and seven loaves of bread, and sealed the stone trapdoor above.

For days I sat among the tombs in despair. But one evening, I heard a rustling sound in the gloom: a wild desert creature—a badger or hyena—had entered the cave through a crack in the rock to scavenge.

I followed the creature through narrow subterranean crevices, crawling through the pitch-black stone for hours, until I saw a ray of celestial light! I emerged onto the sea-beach outside the mountain cliffs, where a passing merchant ship rescued me and carried me back to Baghdad laden with jewels from the ancient tombs.'
moral: Respect local customs, but never surrender hope; perseverance unlocks an exit from the darkest tombs.
